# Computing faster with a full memory:Catalytic algorithms break time-space lower bounds **Abstract** We show that adding "catalytic space" (which starts full and must have its original contents restored at the end of computation) provably speeds up time-and-space-bounded computation. In a natural output model, with _O_(log(_n_)) free space and poly(_n_) catalytic space, we give algorithms for sorting and the discrete Fourier transform running in time _n_1+_o_(1), and an algorithm for matrix multiplication running in time \(n^{\omega+o(1)}\). In the same output model, without additional catalytic space, sorting and DFT are known to require time-space product \(\Omega(n^2)\), and matrix multiplication is known to require time-space product \(\Omega(n^3)\) [BC80; Bea91; Yes84; Abr91]. This is the first unconditional demonstration that (uniform, non-relativized) catalytic logspace algorithms can outperform their (non-catalytic) counterparts. We give several further results relevant to fast catalytic algorithm design. We observe that many applications of sorting, FFT, and fast matrix multiplication (e.g., \(\kappa\)SUM, integer multiplication, and clique counting) can be performed catalytically, giving catalytic logspace algorithms matching (up to subpolynomial factors) the best known unbounded-space runtimes. Furthermore, we give a fast and simple catalytic algorithm for evaluating low-depth threshold circuits, improving the previously known runtime bound from \(\widetilde{O}\left(|C|4^df\right)\) to \(\widetilde{O}\left(|C|2^d\right)\), where |_C_| is the total size (i.e. number of wires) of the circuit, _d_ is the depth, and _f_ is the maximum fan-in. ∗Work supported in part by an NSF GRFP fellowship. †Work supported in part by NSF CCF-2127597 and NSF CCF-2420092. **AI disclosure:** We used several models to search for references, and to proofread the paper. ## 1 Introduction

**Catalytic computing.** In the model of catalytic computing, introduced by Buhrman, Cleve, Koucký, Loff, and Speelman \[BCKLS14\], an algorithm with a small amount of memory (e.g. _O_(log(_n_))-bits, where the input is of length _n_) is augmented with a large amount of "dirty" memory (e.g. poly(_n_) bits). The clean memory is initially empty, but the dirty memory begins full of arbitrary bits the algorithm cannot choose. The algorithm may use both the clean and dirty memory however it sees fit to solve the problem at hand, but it is required to set every bit of the dirty memory back to its initial value when it terminates. (A standard analogy for dirty memory is that one "borrows" a friend’s enormous hard drive full of precious digital memories in order to carry out a computation, but one does not want to lose a friend in the process, so one is careful to restore every bit of the hard drive when done.)

The initial impetus for defining this model was to prove that dirty space is not helpful for computation. This would make intuitive sense: in order to restore every bit of the initial dirty memory contents at the end of computation, one must maintain all of the information throughout the computation, so one cannot "free up" any space in general. However, remarkably, Buhrman, Cleve, Koucký, Loff, and Speelman eventually found ways to make use of dirty space, solving problems that we don’t know how to solve using clean space alone. \[BCKLS14\] defined CL ("catalytic logspace") to be the class of problems solvable with poly(_n_) bits of catalytic space and _O_(log_n_) clean space, and showed the contaminants \(\mathsf{TC}^1\subseteq\mathsf{CL}\subseteq\mathsf{ZPP}\). In particular, NL and BPL are both contained in CL, showing that poly(_n_) dirty space is sufficient to simulate both randomness and nondeterminism in the logspace setting.

This model has generated a large amount of excitement and work among complexity theorists in recent years. We do not aim to give an exhaustive survey here, but some highlights are:

• new algorithms placing more problems in CL (such as \[Pyn25; AM25; AFMSV25; AAV26\]),<tbc>

• new characterizations demonstrating CL is "robust" under natural extensions of the model (such as \[CLMP25; FMST25; KMPS25\]), and<tbc>

• new developments in classical space complexity leveraging catalytic ideas \[CM20; CM24; Wil25\].<tbc>

**Catalytic computation as a means of speeding up low-space algorithms.** For all its successes in complexity theory, so far catalytic computing has not caught on as a major topic of study for the rest of core theoretical computer science. One major reason is that almost all positive results in catalytic computing have been solely focused on minimizing space, while disregarding _running time_. For most TCS researchers, runtime is the gold standard of algorithm performance; space usage is important as a secondary optimization target, but an enormous runtime precludes usefulness. Most known catalytic algorithms are of limited interest from this perspective, as they involve \[BCKLS14\]’s TC<sup>1</sup> simulation, which has a prohibitively large runtime overhead. (For instance, using standard reductions, the resulting CL algorithm for directed _st_-connectivity -- the canonical NL-complete problem -- would have a runtime of \(\widetilde{\Theta}\left(n^8\right)\).)

There has been some recent effort to correct this: Cook and Pyne initiated this direction by giving \(\widetilde{O}\left(n^3m\right)\)- time and \(\widetilde{O}\left(nm\right)\)-time deterministic and randomized CL algorithms, respectively, for directed _st_ connectivity \[CP26\]. Subsequent works have shown that most of the space usage in some existing time-space tradeoff upper bounds can be made catalytic \[CDKMR26\].

In this paper, we give strong additional evidence that dirty space can be useful for designing fast algorithms. We implement several essential tools in modern algorithm design (most centrally, sorting, fast matrix multiplication, and fast Fourier transform) catalytically with little loss in runtime, using only _O_(log_n_) clean space. Near-linear time sorting and Fourier transforms are known to be _unconditionally impossible_ using only \(n^{1-\Omega\left(1\right)}\) workspace in total, so our results demonstrate that dirty space can yield strictly faster algorithms than would be otherwise possible (similar results are known for matrix multiplication) \[BC80; Bea91; Yes84; Abr91\]. (Our algorithm’s output is provided by XORing into a chunk of dirty space, as opposed to the separate-output-tape model under which those lower bounds are usually stated. However, we also show that catalytic algorithms have a strict _unconditional speedup_ in output models where the lower bounds apply.)

## 1.1 Our Results

**Fast catalytic algorithms.** We begin by showing that threshold circuit evaluation, from which (under derandomization assumptions) most known containments in CL follow, can itself be done substantially faster: a single-bit-output circuit of size _w_ and depth _d_ can be evaluated in catalytic logspace in time \(\widetilde{O}\left(w2^d\right)\).<sup>1</sup> (The algorithm of \[BCKLS14\] has runtime \(\widetilde{\Theta}(wf4^d)\), where _f_ is the circuit’s maximum fan-in.) Our algorithm is substantially simpler than that of \[BCKLS14\], relying on a single combinatorial trick as opposed to their algebraic approach.

This approach can also be applied to circuits with _multi-bit_ outputs. When the output is too large to store in the machine’s clean space, we say a catalytic algorithm "computes" a function _g_ if, instead of terminating with the dirty space restored, it terminates with _g(x_) bitwise-XORed into an initial segment of the dirty space. (Note that the dirty space could then be restored by running the algorithm a second time. This output model is particularly natural for designing and composing catalytic algorithms, and hence is our default. See the end of this section, and Section 2, for discussion of alternative models that instead use a separate output tape, which is necessary for comparing to non-catalytic algorithms.) Our circuit evaluation result in this model is as follows:

**Theorem 1.1.** There exists a catalytic algorithm using _O_(log(_w_)+_d_) clean workspace and \(\widetilde{O}\left(w2^d\right)\) time, which takes in a _d_-layer, _w_-wire circuit of symmetric gates, and an input to the circuit, and computes the circuit’s output.

We then show several consequences of fast circuit evaluation:

**Corollary 1.2.** Any problem with size-_S(n_) (uniform) NC<sup>1</sup> circuits has a time-_S(n_)<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> catalytic algorithm using _O_(log(_n_)) clean space.

<sup>1</sup>As is standard, we use \(\widetilde{O}(T(n))\) as shorthand for \(T(n)\cdot poly(logT(n))\).

**Corollary 1.3.** There exists a catalytic algorithm using _O_(log(_n+b_)) clean space and _bn_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time which takes as input a length-_n_ list of _b_-bit numbers, and computes the sorted list.

Corollaries 1.2 and 1.3 follow from direct applications of Theorem 1.1. We show that one can evaluate structured low-degree arithmetic circuits quickly, yielding several further algorithmic consequences:

**Theorem 1.4.** There is a catalytic algorithm which takes in a pair of integer matrices \(A,B\in[\text{poly}(n)]^{n\times n}\) and computes their product _AB_, using _O_(log_n_) clean space and \(n^{\omega+o(1)}\) time.<sup>2</sup>

**Theorem 1.5** (Informal)**.** Over any "reasonable" ring K, there exists a catalytic algorithm which takes in a vector \(x\in\mathcal{K}^n\) and computes the discrete Fourier transform, using _O_(log_n_) clean space and \(n\cdot\text{poly}(logn)\) time.<sup>3</sup>

Using near-linear-time sorting, FFT, and fast matrix multiplication as building blocks, we observe that we can obtain fast catalytic algorithms for a host of downstream applications, for instance:

**Corollary 1.6** (kSUM)**.** Let \(A_1,A_2,\cdots,A_k\) be lists of _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>-bit integers. Let _n_=max_<sub>i</sub>_{|_A<sub>i</sub>_|}. There exists a catalytic algorithm which, using \(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil+o(1)}\) time, \(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil+o(1)}\) catalytic space, and _O_(log_n_) clean space, decides whether there exists a _k_-tuple \((a_1,\cdots,a_k)\in A_1\times\cdots\times A_k\) such that \(a_1+\cdots+a_k=0\) .

**Corollary 1.7** (Triangle counting)**.** Let _G_ be an _n_-vertex simple undirected graph, given as an adjacency matrix. There exists a catalytic algorithm which, using \(n^{\omega+o(1)}\) time, \(n^{\omega+o(1)}\) catalytic space, and _O_(log_n_) clean space, counts the number of triangles in _G_.

We similarly observe that we can attain fast catalytic algorithms for integer multiplication (Corollary 3.2), polynomial multiplication (Corollary 4.7), frequency moments (Corollary 3.4), small universe #3SUM (Corollary 4.8), string matching with wildcards (Corollary 4.9), _k_-path detection (Corollary 4.14), _k_-cycle detection (Corollary 4.15), and 3_k_-clique counting (Corollary 4.12).

**Relationship to lower bounds.** None of the above runtimes are known or believed to be possible for (non- catalytic) algorithms with only _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> free space. So, these are cases where dirty space seems to be genuinely necessary for fast algorithms. Indeed, recall that we know _unconditional_ time-space lower bounds for several of these problems (sorting, DFT, integer multiplication, and matrix multiplication). Our catalytic algorithms achieve runtimes for these problems that are therefore _provably_ impossible for non-catalytic algorithms.

At this point, one might justifiably object that we are not making a fair comparison. These lower bounds are for multi-output functions, where the algorithm is given a separate output tape to which it has limited access (e.g., it must output all of the bits in a single left-to-right pass -- this is known as the "transducer" output model). However, our catalytic algorithms are instead designed to give the output by XORing into the catalytic tape. So it is unclear whether the provable<sup>4</sup> advantage is due to using dirty space to aid computation, or simply due to the different output model.

In Section 5, we therefore give some apples-to-apples comparisons. We define the **_k-output-pass_** output model, where the algorithm makes _k_ left-to-right passes over an output tape, to which it may XOR bits (but may not read existing values). (Note that the case _k_=1 corresponds to the transducer model.) We then observe that all of our catalytic algorithms can be implemented in the 2-output-pass model, and that all known time-space lower bounds (for non-catalytic algorithms) hold in the _k_-output-pass model for any constant _k_. Thus, in this model, having dirty space is provably necessary for achieving fast runtimes.

<sup>2</sup>See further results about matrix multiplications over modular rings in Section 4. <sup>3</sup>See Section 4 for a formal statement. <sup>4</sup>We stress that for any applications to decision problems (e.g. 3SUM or triangle detection), this output distinction is irrelevant, because we could simply copy the first bit of the dirty space into the free space. So, even without any careful model bookkeeping, our results do show an advantage from dirty space, conditional on believable assumptions about the hardness of those problems. The interesting question here is whether we can get something _unconditional_.

It is interesting that our catalytic algorithms require two passes over the output, as opposed to just a single one. We show that this is indeed necessary, by noting the following generalization of the Borodin-Cook method \[BC80; Bea91\] to catalytic space algorithms:

**Theorem 1.8.** For every _catalytic_ 1-output-pass algorithm that takes in a length-_n_ list of log(_n_)-bit integers and outputs the sorted list, we must have \(ST\unknown\Omega(n^2)\), where _S_ and _T_ are the clean space and runtime used by the algorithm, respectively.

It follows (from Theorem 1.8 and our algorithmic results) that catalytic algorithms which make one pass over the output tape are strictly weaker than those which make two passes. However, we note that our results nonetheless show some separation between catalytic and non-catalytic algorithms even with only a single pass over the output (see Proposition 5.3).

## 1.2 Related Work

As mentioned, few prior results in catalytic computing focus on time complexity, but two recent works have begun to explore this direction.

Cook and Pyne \[CP26\] give elegant algorithms for catalytically solving directed connectivity (with _O_(log_n_) clean space) in randomized \(\widetilde{O}(n\cdot m)\) time and deterministic \(\widetilde{O}(n^3\cdot m)\) time, and show how to estimate the probability that a _T_-step random walk ends at a given vertex in \(\widetilde{O}(mT^2/\varepsilon)\) time. These running times are close to the best-known running times achievable with large clean space, but are still at least one polynomial factor away.

Chmel, Dudeja, Koucký, Mertz, and Rajgopal \[CDKMR26\] studied how to transfer classical sublinear-space polynomial-time algorithms into the catalytic model. They give a catalytic algorithm for STCONN running in polynomial time, _O_(log_n_) clean space and \(n/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\mathrm{log}n})}\) catalytic space, matching the best-known space bound; with randomness, their algorithm runs in \(O(m\cdot n^{2+\varepsilon})\) time on _n_-node _m_-edge graphs. They also give polynomial time algorithms for edit distance, LCS, and discrete Fréchet distance using sublinear catalytic space, largely matching known non-catalytic space bounds. However, their focus is primarily on achieving the correct space frontier using only catalytic space, while retaining polynomial time bounds. In contrast, we focus on preserving running times to the greatest extent possible, replacing the usual space of clever classical algorithms with almost entirely catalytic space.

A related space-restricted model is the "in-place" model, where a read-write tape with input _x_ must be overwritten with the output _f(x_), which has received recent attention in the computer algebra literature (e.g. \[Gre25\]) and in complexity theory (\[CGMPS25\]). The algorithms are usually allowed _O_(log_n_) bits of additional clean space, or sometimes _O_(log_n_) algebraic registers. In this model, among many other results, sorting can be computed in _O(n_log_n_) time \[Pas99\] and the Discrete Fourier Transform can be computed in _O(n_log_n_) time \[BE81; Tem91\]. Another variant is the restore model, wherein both the input and output tapes are read-write but the input tape must be restored to its initial contents at the end \[CMR18\]. In this augmented variant, there exist additive accumulation algorithms over fields for the truncated Cooley-Tukey Fast Fourier Transform in _O(n_log_n_) time, Strassen’s matrix multiplication algorithm in _O(n_log<sub>2</sub>(7)) time \[DG24a\], efficient polynomial remainder \[DG24b\], and (more generally) linear accumulation of any in-place computable function \[DG26\].

We make reference to known time-space tradeoff lower bounds, and prove an extension to a catalytic model in Section 5. These are among the small handful of unconditional lower bounds in complexity theory: a landmark result of Borodin and Cook shows that (in any "reasonable" model of computation, e.g. RAM Turing machines, with the transducer output model), the product of space overhead and runtime for any sorting algorithm must be at least \(\Omega(n^2/\mathrm{log}(n))\) \[BC80\], which Beame later improved to \(\Omega(n^2)\) \[Bea91\]. Unconditional time-space-product lower bounds have since been shown for other problems, such as discrete Fourier transform (DFT), integer multiplication, and matrix multiplication \[Yes84; Abr91\].

## 1.3 Proof Intuition

We give here an overview of the proofs of the above results. The main ideas are quite simple, although there are some technical details that one needs to be careful about.

### Evaluating low-depth SYM circuits.

The algorithm given in \[BCKLS14\] for evaluating low-depth threshold circuits involved treating the dirty space as a sequence of "register" values over a finite field. They show that, given an algorithm _A_ which results in a pair of values \(a,b\in\mathbb{F}\) being added into two "registers" of the dirty space, one can use two calls to _A_ to get an algorithm which adds their product _ab_ into another register, while not storing anything except a global timestep counter in-between calls. They give similar constructions for powering, and then use Fermat’s little theorem to show that, given an algorithm _A_ which adds a vector of values \(v\in\mathbb{F}^m\) to a sequence of registers, they can make four calls to _A_ and spend \(\widetilde{O}\left(wf\right)\) additional time in order to add the output of any single layer of threshold gates (with _w_ wires and maximum fan-in _f_) over _v_ to another sequence of registers. Recursing this algorithm then lets them evaluate low-degree circuits of threshold gates.

We use a similar recursive approach, but replace the algebraic methods with a single combinatorial trick, similar to one suggested by Cook \[Coo21\]. Our approach works for circuits of arbitrary symmetric gates (i.e., gates whose output only depends on the number of 1s among input wires), including threshold gates. The underlying idea is as follows. Suppose you can toggle between seeing the value \(\tau\) and the value \(\tau+x\), for some \(\tau,x\in\mathbb{F}_m\). Given a large "helper" array _H_ of dirty values, if you add 1 to \(H[\tau+x-i]\) for every \(i\in S\subseteq\mathbb{F}_m\), then this will increment the value of \(H[\tau]\) if and only if \(x\in S\). Using this fact, we can go from an algorithm adding a vector of bits, to an algorithm adding a _w_-wire layer of symmetric gates over those bits, using only two calls and \(\widetilde{O}\left(w\right)\) time overhead. Recursing this gives an evaluation algorithm running in time \(\widetilde{O}\left(w2^d\right)\) for circuits of depth _d_.

We then observe that this algorithm is near-linear time for circuits of depth _o_(log(_n_)), so obtaining fast catalytic algorithms reduces to designing small, _o_(log(_n_))-depth (uniform) circuits of symmetric gates. In order to get such circuits, we take bounded fan-in circuit models (NC circuits, sorting networks) of depth _O_(log(_n_)), and observe that we can collapse groups of a super-constant number of layers together into constant-depth SYM circuits at only a sub-polynomial blowup in size. This lets us directly convert known results in these models into fast catalytic algorithms.

### Evaluating low-degree arithmetic circuits.

The algebraic approach of \[BCKLS14\] allows evaluating arithmetic circuits, with work which they note grows exponentially with the number of layers of the circuit. But, actually, the work needs only to grow exponentially in the number of layers of the circuit _which involve non-linear product gates_: layers of the circuit which only compute linear functions (i.e. scalar product gates) needn’t contribute. The fast Fourier transform can be written as a small circuit of only linear gates, and any fast matrix multiplication algorithm can (without loss of generality) be written as a small circuit with a single layer of binary products and all other layers linear. So, these algorithms can be simulated with minimal runtime overhead catalytically.

### Time-space tradeoff lower bounds.

The above algorithms are stated in a model where, instead of having a separate output tape, the catalytic algorithm is simply required to XOR the output into an initial portion of its catalytic tape. We observe that any algorithm in this model can be directly simulated in the 2-output- pass model: in the first pass, output an initial portion of the catalytic tape; then, run the original algorithm until it gets to that specified intermediate point, and output the catalytic tape again in the second pass. We therefore get fast algorithms for sorting, DFT, and matrix multiplication in this model.

On the other hand, we observe that any non-catalytic _k_-output-pass algorithm can be converted into a 1- output-pass algorithm using only an _O(k_)-factor increase in space and an \(\widetilde{O}\left(1\right)\)-factor increase in time, by holding _k_ different machine states in memory and simulating all _k_ passes in parallel. So, the lower bounds proven in the transducer (1-output-pass) model directly apply to the 2-output-pass model as well, giving a separation between catalytic and non-catalytic algorithms. In order to get a separation in the transducer<tbc>

model, we note that the above implies that the search problem "given a list _L_, output \((L',L'')\) such that \(L'\oplus L''=\mathsf{SORTED}(L)\)" is possible with low product of time and clean space for catalytic transducers, but not for non-catalytic transducers.

Finally, to get a lower bound for the product of time and clean space against 1-output-pass catalytic algorithms, we directly adapt the Borodin-Cook branching program approach. We consider _catalytic_ branching programs, which have a large number of start vertices, each with corresponding end vertices, and the requirement that computation from a given start vertex must always end at the corresponding end vertex. As in existing lower bounds, we argue that, on a random input, most nodes of the branching program can’t result in outputting too many values. Then, we observe that _every_ path from a start to an end vertex must pass through many nodes that output many values. Since these paths have to be disjoint, this gives a large lower bound on the size of the branching program.

## 2 Preliminaries

We assume basic familiarity with computational complexity \[AB09\] and arithmetic circuit complexity \[SY10\].

**Notation.** We use \[_N_\] to denote the set \(\{1,2,\cdots,N\}\). We write _x_mod_N_ to refer to the representative of _x_’s modular equivalence class in \[_N_\], as opposed to the whole equivalence class. We use base 2 for the logarithm, log_n_:=log<sub>2</sub>(_n_). The set \(\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\cdots\}\) excludes 0.

**Symmetric circuits.** A function \(f:\{0,1\}^m\rightarrow\{0,1\}\) is _symmetric_ if \(f\circ\pi=f\) for every bitwise-permutation \(\pi\). Equivalently, _f_’s output depends only on the number of 1s in its input. (Examples of symmetric functions include `AND`, `OR`, or `MAJORITY`.) A _symmetric circuit_ is a circuit (of arbitrary fan-in) whose gates are all labeled with symmetric functions.

**Catalytic algorithms.** Consider an algorithm with read-only access to an input and read-write access to both a "clean" work-tape, as well as a "dirty" work-tape consisting of _d(n_) bits. We say that such an algorithm is _catalytic_ if, on every input _x_ and every possible initial assignment \(z\in\{0,1\}^{d(n)}\) to dirty space, the algorithm halts with dirty space set to _z_. We design our algorithms under the assumption that the model has RAM access to all of these tapes.

**A note on catalytic space complexity.** It is known (see e.g. \[FLMV05\]) that any RAM computation using time _T=T(n_) accessing memory cells up to index, say, 2<sup>_O(T_)</sup> can be converted to a time \(T\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{log}T)\) equivalent algorithm using _O(T_log_T_) contiguous bits of space. However, we do not yet know of a generic way to perform this conversion for _catalytic_ RAM algorithms running in time _T_. For this reason, we explicitly state the catalytic space bounds for the algorithms throughout this paper. All our algorithms have the feature that the catalytic space complexity is at most the runtime (up to polylog factors).

**Low-space output models.** For space-bounded computation of multi-bit functions, it is crucial to only allow restricted access to the output tape to retain a fair measure of the space. There are several possible ways to restrict the access, which we briefly survey, that could be of material consequence when measuring runtime.<sup>5</sup> For all the subsequent definitions, we say TM _M_ computes function family \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\{0,1\}^\star\) if, for all \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), whenever the input tape is initialized with _x_ the machine halts with _f(x_) on the output tape.

The most restricted model is the bit-by-bit one-way output tape model, where the machine must _commit_ to the value of the _i_th output bit before continuing to the (_i_+1)<sup>st</sup> bit.

<sup>5</sup>All of the following notions are equivalent with respect to space, disregarding time complexity, by simply recording all the changes applied to the _i_th bit of the output tape (for each _i_ at a time) and recomputing as necessary.

**Definition 2.1** (Transducer Output Tape)**.** A space _s=s(n_) **transducer TM** _M_ computing a function family \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\{0,1\}^\star\) has access to:

i) An _n_-bit input tape with a read-only random-access head.<tbc>

ii) An _s_-bit work tape with a read-write random-access head.<tbc>

iii) An output tape initialized to all zeros with a write-only one-way head, which starts in the leftmost cell and can only move right by one cell. Once the machine halts, the output is defined as all the bits up to the head’s current position. (The tape is at most 2<sup>_O(s_)</sup> bits long.)

As the output tape is initialized to zero, moving right by one cell without overwriting the previous one is implicitly equivalent to writing a 0 symbol to that previous cell, in the above definition. Observe both the input and work tapes are random access -- only the output tape is restricted to be one-way access. While the access is one-way, Definition 2.1 does not restrict it to be write-once too (though, without loss of generality, this does not make a difference). Observe that this definition allows the output length to depend on the input itself, not only the input length.

All time-space lower bounds for multi-bit problems appealing to the branching program type defined in the Borodin-Cook argument \[BC80\] apply only to the "append-only" output form. This append-only notion, where we can choose to append some bit to the final output, is equivalent to Definition 2.1. As the time- space lower bounds of \[Yes84; BC80; Abr91; Bea91\] are proven on _R_-way branching programs, a non-uniform analogue of the append-only transducer, they have only been shown to hold for the output tape model of Definition 2.1.<sup>6</sup>

In contrast to clean space algorithms, catalytic ones suggest a different natural output model. Instead of placing the output into an append-only output tape, XOR the output into a chunk of your dirty space. This output model allows for _composition_ of catalytic algorithms which read their input by having it XORed into dirty memory. As these changes to the catalytic tape can be reverted by running the algorithm again, there is no danger of irreparably altering the catalytic tape.

**Definition 2.2** (Dirty-XOR-output model)**.** A clean space _s=s(n_), catalytic space _c=c(n_) **dirty-XOR- output TM** _M_ computing a function family \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\{0,1\}^\star\) has access to:

i) An _n_-bit input tape with a read-only random-access head.<tbc>

ii) An _s_-bit clean work tape with a read-write random-access head.<tbc>

iii) A _c_-bit catalytic work tape (arbitrarily initialized) with a read-write random-access head. Given input _x_, let _k_=|_f(x_)| and \(\tau\) be the first _k_ bits of the dirty tape at initialization. At the end of the computation, the first _k_-bit dirty space chunk should be \(\tau\oplus f(x)\). Each of the other remaining bits must be restored exactly.

The above is restricted only to algorithms with access to dirty space. This motivates a definition of a useful output model applicable to both clean and catalytic space algorithms, in which we can make a comparison between them. The following output definition retains a similar sequential access restriction as Definition 2.1 while incorporating the XOR-access feature of Definition 2.2.

**Definition 2.3** (_k_-output-pass model)**.** A space _s=s(n_) _k_**output-pass TM** _M_ computing function family \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\{0,1\}^\star\) has access to:

i) An _n_-bit input tape with a read-only random-access head.<tbc>

ii) An _s_-bit work tape with a read-write random-access head.<tbc>

<sup>6</sup>Note that a time-space lower bound on non-uniform _R_-way branching programs could be mildly stronger than a time-space lower bound for the transducer model. Aside from being non-uniform, an _R_-way branching program models input query access operations as unit cost and all other operations as _free_. Thus, these time-space lower bounds apply for any space-bounded program with a "reasonable" measure of time. Furthermore, each input cell is assumed to lie in \(\{0,\cdots,R-1\}\) instead of just the boolean set {0,1}.

iii) An output tape, initialized to all zeros, with the following write pattern: _k_ passes of a one-way XOR head. One pass to the output tape consists of a one-way (XOR) head, starting at the leftmost cell and moving right by one cell, that is capable of XORing any value \(b\in\{0,1\}\) to the current cell. To conclude one pass, the head position is reset to the leftmost cell -- this resetting is only done (at most) _k_-1 times. Once the machine halts, the output is defined as all the bits up to the _rightmost_ accessed head position over the entire computation. (The tape is at most 2<sup>_O(s_)</sup> bits long.)

Note this definition does not allow for overwriting bits of the output tape. As XORing _b_=0 into any bit keeps that bit the same and XORing by _b_=1 flips it, we can equivalently think of Definition 2.3 as allowing the machine to flip bits of the output tape in a multi-pass fashion. As bit-flips (XORs) can be undone by simply flipping (XORing) again, any machine in the above model will only modify the output tape _reversibly_ -- run the machine again to undo.

Observe that for _k_=1 the _k_-output-pass model (Definition 2.3) is, in fact, equivalent in power to the transducer model (Definition 2.1), so the transducer is a special case of the _k_-pass model.<sup>7</sup>

**Hash functions.** We define perfect hash families and note small such families can be constructed efficiently. These are used to obtain _k_-path and _k_-cycle algorithms in Section 4.3.

**Definition 2.4** (Perfect Hashing)**.** Fix a universe _U_. A _k_-perfect hash family H_<sub>U,m</sub>_ is a set of functions of the form \(h:U\rightarrow[m]\) with the following property. For any set \(S\subseteq U\) with |_S_|=_k_ there exists an \(h\in\mathcal{H}_{U,m}\) such that _h_ maps _S_ injectively onto \[_m_\].

**Lemma 2.5** (Uniform perfect hash, full table)**.** \[SS90; FKS84\] Let _n,k_ be positive integers. There exists a _k_-perfect hash family mapping from universe \[_n_\] to \[_m_\] with the following properties.

• Each function in the family is specified using _b=O(k_+loglog_n_) bits.<tbc>

• We can iterate through all functions in the family in 2<sup>_O(k_)</sup>poly(log_n_) time and _O_(log_n+k_) space.<tbc>

• For input \(x\in[n]\) and function _h_ in the family, we can compute _h(x_) in _O_(log(_n+k_)) space and poly(log(_n+k_)) time.

**Uniformity.** We define a natural notion of uniform arithmetic circuits and boolean circuits that will be useful for our catalytic algorithm applications. In short, a circuit family {_C<sub>n</sub>_} is uniform in our sense if the gate and wire information can be computed in polylog time and logspace, and (when arithmetic) every bit of every scalar on every wire can be determined in polylog time and logspace. <sup>8</sup>

Let {_C<sub>n</sub>_} be a polynomial-size arithmetic circuit family, and fix a ring K. Let _S<sup>gates</sup>(n_), \(S_\ell^{wires}(n)\), and _S<sup>wires</sup>(n_) be the total number of gates in _C<sub>n</sub>_, the total number of wires in layer \(\ell\) of _C<sub>n</sub>_, and the total number of wires in _C<sub>n</sub>_, respectively.

**Definition 2.6** (Succinctly-uniform arithmetic circuits)**.** We say that arithmetic family {_C<sub>n</sub>_} is **succinctly- uniform** if there is a poly(log_n_)-time, _O_(log_n_)-space algorithm such that, given \((i,j,\ell)\) in binary (where \(i,j,\ell\in[\text{poly}(n)]\)) and \(m\in[\lceil log|\mathcal{K}|\rceil]\) in binary, the algorithm outputs:

• The following information about the _i_<sup>th</sup> gate residing in the \(\ell^\mathrm{th}\) layer of _C_, denoted \(g_{i,\ell}\):<tbc>

– \(\text{incoming}(i,\ell,j)\): encodes the index _k_ of the gate in layer \(\ell-1\) corresponding to the _j_<sup>th</sup> incoming wire to \(g_{i,\ell}\), as well as the _m_<sup>th</sup> low-order bit of the scalar \(\alpha_j\in\mathcal{K}\) attached to the wire if \(g_{i,\ell}\) is linear.<tbc>

**–** \(\text{in.degree}(i,\ell)\): The in-degree of gate \(g_{i,\ell}\).<tbc>

<sup>7</sup>Indeed, on an output tape initialized to zeros, XORing bit \(b\in\{0,1\}\) once onto the tape is equivalent to overwriting by _b_. <sup>8</sup>For circuits, this is distinct from standard logspace uniformity in that the usual definition imposes no restriction on the runtime (aside from the polynomial bound implied by any logspace algorithm). Our definition ensures we can simulate the circuits with little unnecessary time overhead.

• \(S_\ell^{gates}\): the number of gates in layer \(\ell\) of _C_.

This is defined analogously for boolean circuits.

## 3 Evaluating Low-Depth Circuits of Symmetric Gates

In this section, we give a fast and simple version of the circuit evaluation algorithm from \[BCKLS14\], and note several algorithmic applications of fast circuit evaluation.

### 3.1 Fast SYM Circuit Evaluation

**Theorem 1.1.** There exists a catalytic algorithm using _O_(log(_w_)+_d_) clean workspace and \(\widetilde{O}\left(w2^d\right)\) time, which takes in a _d_-layer, _w_-wire circuit of symmetric gates, and an input to the circuit, and computes the circuit’s output.

_Proof._ By increasing the number of wires by at most a factor of _d_, we can assume that the circuit is _layered_, in that all gates only read the outputs of gates on the previous layer. We also assume without loss of generality that _w_, and all gate fan-ins, are powers of two. (Otherwise, simply add dummy gates and wires to the circuit to make this the case.) We divide the catalytic space into "registers", each of which stores a value from \[_w_\].

For each gate _g_ of the circuit, we assign an associated "output register", and _f<sub>g</sub>_ associated "helper registers", where _f<sub>g</sub>_ is _g_’s fan-in. We will use _R<sub>g</sub>_ and \(R_g^{(1)},\dots,R_g^{(f_g)}\) to refer to the values held by these registers, respectively, at a given point in time. Let \(\tau_g\) and \(\tau_g^{(1)},\dots,\tau_g^{(f_g)}\) denote the initial values of these registers prior to any computation.

Our goal will be to set every gate’s output register to \(\tau_g+b_i\text{mod}w\), where _b<sub>i</sub>_ is the value (0 or 1) outputted by the gate when the circuit reads its input<sup>10</sup>. We say a gate is "computed" if \(R_g=\tau_g+b_i\text{mod}w\), and "reset" if \(R_g=\tau_g\). (Note that it could also be in neither of these states.)

As in \[BCKLS14\], we do this computation recursively. That is, we assume we have a reversible algorithm \(A_\ell\) that computes all of the output registers on level \(\ell\), and use this algorithm as a subroutine to yield a reversible algorithm \(A_{\ell+1}\) that computes all of the output registers on level \(\ell+1\). In order to keep the space usage small, we ensure that we always completely erase the clean space before each<tbc>

<sup>9</sup>Therefore, by convention, input gates always have all incoming wires be \(\perp\). <sup>10</sup>Observe that, if we can do so, then we can also write the answer onto an XOR-only output tape while resetting the catalytic space: First, XOR the least-significant bits of all of the final layer’s output registers into the output. Then, run our algorithm. Then, do this XOR again. Finally, run our algorithm in reverse to reset all of the gates.

subroutine call, except for a single global counter that lets the machine know which step of the algorithm to perform. This means that the total clean space usage will be log(# steps), for the counter, plus \(\mathrm{max}_\ell\)(clean space overhead at the \(\ell\)th layer of recursion).

Our algorithm \(A_{\ell+1}\) proceeds as follows (erasing the clean space in between each step):

i) For each gate _g_ on layer \(\ell+1\) of the circuit, determine \(i_g=\sum_{g^\prime|g^\prime\text{is an input gate to}g}R_{g^\prime}\mathrm{mod}f_g\), and set \(R_g\leftarrow R_g-R_g^{(i_g)}\mathrm{mod}w\).<tbc>

ii) Run _A_.<tbc>

iii) For each gate _g_ on layer \(\ell+1\), determine \(j_g=\sum_{g^\prime|g^\prime\text{is an input gate to}g}R_{g^\prime}\mathrm{mod}f_g\). Now, for every value _t_ such that _g_ would output 1 if exactly _t_ inputs were 1, set \(R_g^{j_g-t}\leftarrow R_g^{j_g-t}+1\mathrm{mod}w\).<tbc>

iv) Run _A_ in reverse.<tbc>

v) Once more, for each gate _g_ on layer \(\ell+1\), determine \(i_g=\sum_{g^\prime|g^\prime\text{is an input gate to}g}R_{g^\prime}\mathrm{mod}f_g\). This time, set \(R_g\leftarrow R_g+R_g^{(i_g)}\mathrm{mod}w\).

We claim this will result in every gate on the \(\ell+1\)st layer being computed. Observe that the values of _i<sub>g</sub>_ computed in steps i) and v) will be identical, and that the value of _j<sub>g</sub>_ computed in step iii) will be equal to _i<sub>g</sub>_+(# of 1s among input wires to _g_)mod_f<sub>g</sub>_. So, step iii) will increment \(R_g^{i_g}\) by 1 if and only if the number of 1s among inputs to _g_ would make _g_ output 1. Otherwise, \(R_g^{i_g}\) will remain unchanged. Since we subtract off from _R<sub>g</sub>_ the initial value of \(R_g^{i_g}\), and then add back in the final value of \(R_g^{i_g}\), this procedure will result in _g_ being computed.

Observe also that each step can be computed with low space overhead (we simply do memory lookups and compute running sums), and that this sequence of operations is reversible (every step either performs some linear operations, based on the indices specified by some registers that remain constant, or else consists of calling _A_). To bound the runtime, observe that \(A_{\ell+1}\) makes two recursive calls to \(A_\ell\), and then for each gate performs a number of register lookups and additions proportional to that gate’s fan-in, meaning at most _O(w_) total such operations. So, the overall runtime is at most \(\widetilde{O}\left(w2^d\right)\).

## 3.2 Application: Integer Multiplication

The ability to quickly evaluate low-depth circuits of symmetric gates is in fact a very useful algorithmic tool. Observe that Theorem 1.1 gives an algorithm with runtime near-linear in the circuit size whenever _d=o_(log_w_). We use this fact here to directly obtain near-linear-time catalytic logspace algorithms for several fundamental problems.

First, we observe that this gives us a near-linear-time algorithm for evaluating any NC<sup>1</sup> circuit:

**Lemma 3.1.** Given a fan-in 2 boolean circuit of size _S_ and depth _O_(log(_S_)), there exists a catalytic algorithm which computes the circuit’s output using _O_(log(_S_)) clean workspace and _S_<sup>1+_O_(1/loglog(_S_))</sup> time.

_Proof._ We observe that any such circuit can be easily converted into a SYM circuit of depth log(_S)/_loglog(_S_) and size _S_<sup>1+_O_(1/loglog(_S_))</sup>. That is, we show how to replace loglog(_S)/_100 layers of fan-in-2 gates with _O_(1) layers of arbitrary fan-in SYM gates. Observe that an output at the end of those loglog(_S)/_100 layers can only depend on at most 2<sup>loglog(_S)/_100</sup>=log(_S_)<sup>1/100</sup> inputs. We can build a constant-depth SYM circuit which checks whether those inputs equal each of the 2<sup>log(_S_)</sup><sup>1/100</sup> possible settings, and returns the correct value for each. This requires 2<sup>_O_(log(_S_)<sup>1/100</sup>)</sup> wires. So, using 2<sup>_O_(log(_S_)<sup>1/100</sup>)</sup> wires for each gate of the original circuit, we can replace every loglog(_S)/_100 layers of the original circuit with circuits of this form. The overall statement holds by plugging that resulting circuit into Theorem 1.1.

From this, we immediately get fast catalytic algorithms for any problems for which we know small NC<sup>1</sup> circuits. For instance:

**Corollary 3.2.** There exists a catalytic algorithm using _O_(log(_n_)) clean space and _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time which takes as input a pair of _n_-bit integers and computes their product.

_Proof._ The classic Schönhage-Strassen algorithm for integer multiplication gives a (succinctly uniform) NC<sup>1</sup> circuit of size _O(n_log(_n_)loglog(_n_)) \[SS71; Weg87\]. Applying Lemma 3.1 to this circuit yields the result. \(\blacksquare\)

Recall that Schönhage-Strassen works by computing a discrete Fourier transform over Z/(2_<sup>m</sup>_+1)Z -- the same argument as above shows that such DFTs can be performed in near-linear time catalytically. As we observe in Section 4, in fact there exists an algorithm with the even faster runtime \(\widetilde{O}(n)\), over any ring with efficiently-computable operations, which in turn also gives \(\widetilde{O}(n)\)-time polynomial multiplication.

## 3.3 Application: Sorting

We do not know small NC<sup>1</sup> circuits for sorting lists of integers, but fortunately, if we are somewhat more careful, we can nonetheless also apply Theorem 1.1 here:

**Corollary 3.3.** There exists a catalytic algorithm using _O_(log(_n+b_)) clean space and _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>_b_ time which takes as input a length-_n_ list of _b_-bit numbers, and computes the sorted list.

_Proof._ Recall that there exists an _O_(log(_n_))-depth _sorting network_ \[AKS83\]. A sorting network operates over _n_ wires, and consists of "comparators" which swap the values of two wires if they are out of sorted order.

If this network was converted into a fan-in 2 Boolean circuit, each comparator would require depth log(_b_), so the overall circuit would have depth _O_(log(_n_)log(_b_)), which is much too high to apply Lemma 3.1. However, we can nonetheless produce a _o_(log(_n_))-depth, _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>_b_-size SYM circuit, by a similar approach to the proof of that lemma. That is, we show how to evaluate loglog(_n)/_100 layers of a sorting network using a constant- depth SYM circuit with _O(bn_<sup>1+1/loglog(_n_)</sup>) wires.

Suppose we have written down the values on all of the wires prior to this sequence of layers, and want to compute the value of one of the wires after the sequence of layers. This wire’s output depends on at most 2<sup>loglog(_n)/_100</sup>=log<sup>1/100</sup>(_n_) of the initial values. Observe that there are only \(log^{1/100}(n)!\le 2^{log^{1/50}(n)}\) possible orderings of those log<sup>1/100</sup>(_n_) many values, and that the ordering of those values is sufficient to determine which of them should be written to the output wire. Now, for a given candidate ordering, there exists a _O(b_2<sup>log<sup>1/50</sup>(_n_)</sup>)-wire AC<sup>0</sup> circuit which evaluates whether the values are thus ordered: we can check whether a given pair of values is in the correct order in _O(b_) size and depth _O_(1) \[CSV84\], so we simply do all of these checks in parallel and take their AND. So, to compute the _i_th bit on output value of the wire, we can simply compute in parallel for each initial value ordering whether that ordering is correct, and then take the OR over all orderings of "this initial value ordering is correct AND the _i_th bit of the value which would get output under this initial value ordering is a 1".

This overall gives a SYM circuit for sorting with depth _O_(log(_n)/_loglog(_n_)) and size \(O(nlog(n)\cdot b2^{log^{1/50}(n)})=O(bn^{1+o(1)})\). Since the AKS sorting network is DLOGTIME uniform, and the identity of a gate or wire in the above constructed circuit can be computed in logarithmic space and _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup> time given the original sorting network, we can apply Theorem 1.1 to evaluate it in time _bn_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>. \(\blacksquare\)

We observe that by composing catalytic algorithms one can use these results to get fast algorithms for decision (and counting) problems:

**Corollary 1.6** (kSUM)**.** Let \(A_1,A_2,\cdots,A_k\) be lists of _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>-bit integers. Let _n_=max_<sub>i</sub>_{|_A<sub>i</sub>_|}. There exists a catalytic algorithm which, using \(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil+o(1)}\) time, \(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil+o(1)}\) catalytic space, and _O_(log_n_) clean space, decides whether there exists a _k_-tuple \((a_1,\cdots,a_k)\in A_1\times\cdots\times A_k\) such that \(a_1+\cdots+a_k=0\) .

_Proof._ The standard reduction from kSUM to 2SUM is efficiently computable, in the sense that a given bit of the kSUM instance can be computed in log(_n_) space and polylog(_n_) time given read access to the 2SUM instance \[Eri95\]. So, it suffices to give an _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>-time, _O_(log_n_) clean space, catalytic algorithm for 2SUM. This follows from the standard reduction from 2SUM to sorting, which can be implemented catalytically.

That is, take one of the lists, negate all of the elements in it, add some small \(\varepsilon\) to all of them, and merge it with the other list. Then, use the _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup>-time CL algorithm for sorting. Finally, observe that there is a near-linear-size TC<sup>0</sup> circuit which returns whether any adjacent elements of a list differ by exactly \(\varepsilon\) -- this yields a near-linear-time CL algorithm by Theorem 1.1, which reads its input via XORing into the catalytic tape a constant number of times, and hence can be composed with the previous algorithm. The composition of these algorithms will decide 2SUM.

We note that a similar idea<sup>11</sup> will also allow computing #kSUM in \(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil+o(1)}\)-time CL. A modification of this #2SUM construction, instead taking the _k_th power of the element count in equal-value blocks, gives:

**Corollary 3.4.** Let _A_ be a list of _n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup>-bit integers. Let _n_=|_A_| and let _k\>_1 be a constant. There exists a catalytic algorithm computing the _k_th frequency moment

\(F_k=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}(f_i)^k,\)

where _f<sub>i</sub>_ is the frequency of value _i_ in _A_. This algorithm takes _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time, _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> catalytic space, and _O_(log_n_) clean space.

We note that while \[BCCPV26; KKK26\] show there exist \(\widetilde{O}(n)\) time catalytic algorithms computing frequency moments, their algorithms would use catalytic space proportional to the size of the universe (i.e. they would only get a bound of 2<sup>_n_<sup>_o_(1)</sup></sup> catalytic space).

## 4 Evaluating Low-Degree Arithmetic Circuits

In this section, we observe that with some modifications the original \[BCKLS14\] approach for circuit evaluation will actually allow fast evaluation of even high-depth arithmetic circuits, so long as most layers consist only of linear operations. This allows us to obtain fast catalytic algorithms for Fourier transforms, matrix multiplication, and applications thereof.

### 4.1 Fast Low-Multiplicative-Depth Circuit Evaluation

**Definition 4.1.** For a ring K, an #NC(K) circuit has the following gateset:

i) fan-in 2 addition gates,<tbc>

ii) fan-in 2 product gates, and<tbc>

iii) fan-in 1 "\(\times x\)" and "+_x_" gates for each constant \(x\in\mathcal{K}\).

We say that such a circuit has **_multiplicative depth_** _d_ if its gates are presented grouped into layers such that gates in each layer depend only on gates in previous layers, and such that at most _d_ of those layers involve (fan-in 2) product gates.

We show that we can evaluate succinctly uniform #NC(K) circuits in near-linear time so long as they have sublogarithmic multiplicative depth, and so long as the ring operations are efficiently computable.

<sup>11</sup>One can similarly reduce to #2SUM, and begin by sorting, but now in order to construct a near-linear-size, _o_(log(_n_))- depth threshold circuit which performs the relevant counting step, one needs to be somewhat more careful. One can get this construction e.g. by breaking up into blocks of size _n_<sup>1/loglog(_n_)</sup>, spending _n_<sup>2/loglog(_n_)</sup> time counting in each block, and recurring loglog(_n_) times, as Allender and Koucký do for hardness magnification \[AK10\].

Specifically, the ring requirements are as follows, following \[BCKLS14, Section 4.1\] but with a further time constraint:

**Definition 4.2** (\[BCKLS14\], Section 4.1)**.** Let K=K_<sub>n</sub>_ be a family of rings. We say K is **(_S,T)-uniform_** if there exists a bijection _e<sub>n</sub>_ mapping K_<sub>n</sub>_ to the lexicographically first |K| strings of \(\{0,1\}^{\lceil log|\mathcal{K}_n|\rceil}\), such that there exist _S(n_)-space, _T(n_)-time algorithms for the following operations:

• On read-only input (1_<sup>n</sup>,e(u),e(v_)), output (each bit of) \(e(u\circ v)\), for operation \(\circ\in\{+,-,\times\}\).<tbc>

• On read-only input (1_<sup>n</sup>,e(v_)) and _e(u_) on a read-write tape, transform _e(u_) in place into _e(u+v_).<tbc>

• On input (1_<sup>n</sup>_), output (each bit of) _e_(-1)_,e_(0)_,e_(1) and |K_<sub>n</sub>_|.

Note that, for instance, \(\{\mathbb{Z}/m_n\mathbb{Z}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is \((O(loglogm),\mathsf{polylog}(m))\)-uniform for any uniform sequence \(\{m_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\). We have the following:

**Theorem 4.3.** Let K be an (_S,T_)-uniform ring. There exists a catalytic algorithm using time \(\widetilde{O}\left(w3^dT\right)\), clean space _O_(log(_w_)+_d_+log(_T_)+_S_), and dirty space \(\widetilde{O}\left(wlog|\mathcal{K}_n|\right)\), which takes in a #NC(K_<sub>n</sub>_) circuit with _w_ wires and multiplicative depth _d_, and a setting of all of the input wires to the circuit, and computes the value of all of the circuit’s output wires.

_Proof._ The proof is essentially identical to that of \[BCKLS14\], except that we make a distinction between different types of multiplication gates (linear and non-linear) and adjust accordingly. We think of the dirty space as consisting of a sequence of "registers", each holding a value over K_<sub>n</sub>_. Note that, if |K_<sub>n</sub>_| is a power of 2, this is trivial to do, but otherwise it is non-obvious one can treat the dirty space this way. Nonetheless, \[CDKMR26\] shows how, at polylogarithmic overhead in time and dirty space, one can assume without loss of generality that one has access to such registers over K_<sub>n</sub>_. (This follows by compressing the dirty space whenever a large block of tape cells contains no value in the appropriate range -- see their Appendix A. Their algorithm requires a pre-processing and post-processing phase, so we assume our entire procedure below happens between these.)

Let \(\tau_i\in\mathcal{K}_n\) denote the initial contents of the _i_th register, and _R<sub>i</sub>_ denote the value currently held at a given point in the algorithm. As in Theorem 1.1, we say that the _i_th gate’s value is "reset" if \(R_i=\tau_i\), and "computed" if \(R_i=\tau_i+v_i\), where _v<sub>i</sub>_ is that gate’s output in the arithmetic circuit. Assume we have a reversible algorithm \(A_\ell\) that results in all of the gates up to and including the \(\ell\)th multiplicative layer being converted from "reset" to "computed", and leaves the clean space empty except for a single global time counter. We give a reversible algorithm \(A_{\ell+1}\) which makes 3 calls to \(A_\ell\) and takes \(\widetilde{O}\left(wT\right)\) time. This algorithm will require further helper registers \(R_i^{(1)}\) and \(R_i^{(2)}\) for every _i_ corresponding to a product gate.

The algorithm proceeds as follows (erasing the clean space after each step):

i) For each gate _i_ (in order of layers, from the output layer backwards):<tbc>

• If _i_ is an addition gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i-R_j-R_k\), where _j_ and _k_ are the two input gates.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a \(\times x\) gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i-R_j\times x\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a +_x_ gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i-R_j\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a product gate on the \(\ell+1\)st layer of the circuit, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_jR_k+R_jR_i^{(1)}+R_i^{(2)}R_k\), where _j_ and _k_ are the two input gates.<tbc>

ii) Run \(A_\ell\).<tbc>

iii) For each gate _i_ (in order of layers, from the input layer forwards):<tbc>

• If _i_ is an addition gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_j+R_k\), where _j_ and _k_ are the two input gates.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a \(\times x\) gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_j\times x\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a +_x_ gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_j+x\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a product gate on the \(\ell+1\)st layer of the circuit, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_jR_k\), set \(R_i^{(1)}\leftarrow R_i^{(1)}+R_k\), and set \(R_i^{(2)}\leftarrow R_i^{(2)}+R_j\), where _j_ and _k_ are the two input gates.

iv) For each gate _i_ (in order of layers, from the output layer backwards):<tbc>

• If _i_ is an addition gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i-R_j-R_k\), where _j_ and _k_ are the two input gates.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a \(\times x\) gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i-R_j\times x\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a +_x_ gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i-R_j-x\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

v) Run \(A_\ell\) in reverse.<tbc>

vi) For each gate _i_ (in order of layers, from the input layer forwards):<tbc>

• If _i_ is an addition gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_j+R_k\), where _j_ and _k_ are the two input gates.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a \(\times x\) gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_j\times x\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a +_x_ gate in-between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st multiplicative layers, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i+R_j\), where _j_ is the input gate.<tbc>

• If _i_ is a product gate on the \(\ell+1\)st layer of the circuit, set \(R_i\leftarrow R_i-R_jR_i^{(1)}-R_i^{(2)}R_k\), where _j_ and _k_ are the two input gates.

Observe that, for any non-product gate _i_ between the \(\ell\)th and \(\ell+1\)st layers, _i_ will be reset initially, computed after step iii), and then reset again after step vi). By the same analysis as in \[BCKLS14\], all of the product gates will therefore end up computed at the end of this program. All of the steps are reversible, so we now have a reversible algorithm \(A_{\ell+1}\), which makes two calls to \(A_\ell\) plus an additional \(\widetilde{O}\left(wT\right)\) runtime overhead, and results in all of the gates on multiplicative layer \(\ell+1\) being computed. Note that this algorithm by default wouldn’t result in the gates prior to multiplicative layer \(\ell+1\) being computed. However, we can easily fix this by running \(A_\ell\) again. If the final tail of layers in the circuit are all linear (the last layer isn’t multiplicative), we can compute up to those layers by simply running steps i), \(A_\ell\) (where \(\ell\) is the last multiplicative layer), and iii) on them.

Now, evaluating _A<sub>d</sub>_ will take runtime \(\widetilde{O}\left(3^dwT\right)\), and clean space _O_(log(_w_)+_d_+log(_T_)) (for the global time counter) plus _O(S_) (for the individual register operations). _A<sub>d</sub>_ results in the circuit’s outputs being added into the dirty registers as elements of K_<sub>n</sub>_ -- we observe in Appendix A that such a program can efficiently be converted into one that instead bitwise-XORs the circuit outputs into the dirty space. \(\blacksquare\)

## 4.2 Application: Fourier Transforms

One particularly useful corollary of Theorem 4.3 is the fact that we can implement fast Fourier transforms catalytically:

**Definition 4.4** (Principal Root of Unity)**.** \[BP94, p.11\] Let K be a finite ring and 1_\<m\<_|K|. \(\omega_m\in\mathcal{K}\) is a _principal root of unity_ of order _m_ iff:

• \((\omega_m)^m=1\).<tbc>

• \(\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(\omega_m)^{ij}=0\) for all \(1\le i<m\).<tbc>

**Definition 4.5** (Discrete Fourier Transform, DFT)**.** Let \(\mathbf{x}=(x_0,\cdots,x_{n-1})^T\in\mathcal{K}^n\) be a column vector over the ring K. Define the matrix

\(F_n=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c c }
1 & 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
1 & \omega_n^1 & \omega_n^2 & \cdots & \omega_n^{n-1} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots &  &  \\
1 & \omega_n^{1(n-1)} & \omega_n^{2(n-1)} & \cdots & \omega_n^{(n-1)(n-1)}
\end{array}\right)\)

in \(\mathcal{K}^{n\times n}\) where \(\omega_n\) is an _n_th order principal root of unity in K. The discrete Fourier transform is the linear transformation \(\mathbf{x}\mapsto F_n\cdot\mathbf{x}\).

**Corollary 4.6.** Over any (_S,T_)-uniform ring K=K_<sub>n</sub>_, for _n_ a power of 2, if K admits a principal _n_th root of unity, with both that root and its inverse computable in _S_ space and _T_ time, then there exists a catalytic algorithm running in time \(\widetilde{O}\left(nT\right)\), clean space _O_(log(_n_)+log(_T_)+_S_), and dirty space \(\widetilde{O}\left(nlog|\mathcal{K}|\right)\), which takes as input a sequence \(x\in\mathcal{K}^n\), and outputs the discrete Fourier transform _F<sub>n</sub>x_.

_Proof._ The classic Number Theoretic Transform algorithm and its inverse are directly implementable as #NC(K) circuits of multiplicative depth 0 -- i.e., with only addition and scalar multiplication gates -- assuming a principal _n_th root of unity and its inverse are available as constants \[CLRS09, Section 30.2\]. Theorem 4.3 therefore allows such circuits to be evaluated catalytically with only polylogarithmic overhead in time complexity.

We could have obtained a similar result in Section 3, but recall that there our algorithm would have required _n_<sup>1+_o_(1)</sup> time, as opposed to \(\widetilde{O}\left(n\right)\), and would have been difficult to make work over as general a class of rings, since we would have to implement the ring operations themselves as sufficiently low-depth symmetric circuits.

## 5 Time-Space Tradeoff Lower Bounds

We now discuss how the above algorithmic results relate to time-space tradeoff _lower bounds_. Although our algorithms are stated in an output model that involves XORing into the dirty tape, we show that we can instead describe them in separate-tape-output models, where existing lower bounds imply that dirty space is provably necessary for fast algorithms.

### 5.1 Separating catalytic and non-catalytic time-and-space-bounded complexity

Recall that our catalytic algorithms are stated in the _dirty-XOR_ output model. We observe that they could equivalently be stated in the 2-output-pass output model with no asymptotic loss in space or runtime.

**Lemma 5.1.** Assume there exists a clean space _S_, catalytic space _C_, and time _T_ algorithm _A_ which computes \(f=f_n:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\{0,1\}^m\) in the dirty-XOR output model. Then, there exists a clean space _O(S_), dirty space _C_, time _O(T_) algorithm which given _x_ outputs _f(x_) on a 2-pass XOR output tape.

_Proof._ First, output the first _m_ bits of the catalytic tape. Then, simulate _A_ to completion. XOR in the new first _m_ bits of the catalytic tape in a second pass. Finally, simulate _A_ a second time in order to reset the dirty space.

We then show that, for algorithms without catalytic space, the 2-output-pass XOR output model is equivalent to the transducer (i.e., 1-pass) output model. In fact, the proof of Lemma 5.2 below also applies to a modified _k_-output-pass model where _both_ XOR-into and overwrite instructions are allowed.

**Lemma 5.2.** Let \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) be a constant. Given any space _S_, time _T_ algorithm _A_ which outputs \(f=f_n:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\{0,1\}^\star\) in the _k_-output-pass output model, there exists a space _O(kS_), time _O(T_) algorithm which computes _f_ in a single pass.

We will thus record _k_ distinct configurations, each of which takes _O(S_) space to write down. Given these configurations, we now proceed in parallel: simulate each of them until they output their first bit, then XOR all of those bits together and output them. Proceed likewise for the second bit, and so on.

So, this is implied by our above results. \(\blacksquare\)

## 5.2 Separating 1-pass and 2-pass catalytic time-and-space-bounded complexity

Given that the _k_-pass XOR and 1-pass XOR models are equivalent for constant _k_ (up to constant factors in time and space) without dirty space, one might ask whether they are similarly equivalent for catalytic algorithms. We show that this is unconditionally false: while catalytic algorithms can quickly sort in the 2-pass XOR model, they cannot do so in only a single pass.

**Theorem 5.4.** For any catalytic transducer that takes in a length-_n_ list of log(_n_)-bit integers and outputs the sorted list, we must have \(ST\unknown\Omega(n^2)\), where _S_ and _T_ are the clean space and runtime used by the algorithm, respectively.

_Proof._ The proof we give directly follows Beame’s time-space tradeoff lower bound in the case with no catalytic space \[Bea91\].

Recall the notion of a _catalytic branching program_ operating over a list \[GKM15\]. A standard branching program is a directed acyclic graph, where each node is labeled with an index of the list to read, and has an outgoing edge corresponding to each possible value that could be read at each index. Some nodes are also marked with one or more _output values_. Given an input list, one can produce an output list by starting at a designated "input node", querying the input list in the specified place, following the corresponding out-edge, outputting any output values specified by the new node, and repeating. In a _catalytic_ branching program, there are instead _several_ nodes designated as "start nodes", each with a corresponding "end node". We require that the output is always correct regardless of which of these start nodes the program begins at, and that the program always ends at the end node corresponding to the start node where it began. Say that a branching program is "layered" if nodes can be partitioned into layers such that each edge connects nodes in adjacent layers. Let the _length_ of a branching program be the number of layers, and the _amortized size_ be the number of nodes divided by the number of start nodes.

Observe that, if we have a time-_T_, clean-space _S_ catalytic transducer for a problem, we immediately get a length-_O(T_), amortized width-2<sup>_O(S_)</sup> catalytic branching program for that problem. (To see this, let each possible state of the Turing machine correspond to a node of the branching program, let the edges correspond to the transitions the machine would perform, and let the start and end nodes correspond to the machine in the start and end states with the clean space empty. If _w_, _c_, and _f_ are the number of bits of workspace, catalytic space, and finite Turing machine control respectively used by the machine, then this catalytic branching program will have 2<sup>_w+c+f_</sup> nodes and 2_<sup>c</sup>_ start nodes.) So, it suffices to show that sorting does not have a catalytic branching program of amortized size 2_<sup>S</sup>_ and length _T_ for any \(ST\unknown o(n^2)\).

In fact, we show that the _unique elements_ problem, of outputting (in an arbitrary order) all of the elements of a list that appear exactly once, does not have such a catalytic branching program. As a time-_T_, clean-space _S_ transducer for sorting can easily be converted into a time-_O(T_), clean-space _O(S_) transducer for unique elements, this gives the desired result.

Fix some catalytic branching program with _T_ layers, _x_ start vertices, and \(x\cdot 2^S\) total vertices. For a node _v_ in the branching program, and an input list _L_, we will say (_v,L_) is _good_ if, when starting from _v_ and taking _n/_2 branching program steps, the program outputs at least _n_<sup>2</sup>/400_T_ distinct values in \[_n_\], each of which appears at most once in _L_.

**Claim 5.5.** For any node _v_ in any catalytic branching program, if we choose _L_ uniformly at random from \[_n\]<sup>n</sup>_, we have \(Pr_L[(v,L)\text{is good}]\le(1-\Omega(1))^{n^2/T}\).

_Proof._ We can imagine randomly choosing values of _L_ one-at-a-time as the branching program queries them. Once _n/_2 steps have been taken, there would then remain at least _n/_2 indices of _L_ which have yet to be determined, all of which will be chosen uniformly and independently from \[_n_\]. So, for any value \(y\in[n]\) that has been output after these steps, there is at least a \(1-(1-1/n)^{n/2}\ge\Omega(1)\) chance that _y_ appears at least twice in _L_. These events are anti-correlated, so if we output more than _n_<sup>2</sup>/400_T_ values, then there is at most a \((1-\Omega(1))^{n^2/400T}\) probability that none of them appear more than once in the list.

**Claim 5.6.** Suppose a given catalytic branching program, with _x_ start vertices, correctly solves unique elements on a given list \(L\in[n]^n\), and _L_ contains at least _n/_100 unique elements. Then, the branching program must contain at least _x_ vertices _v_ such that (_v,L_) is good.

_Proof._ In order for a given computation path in the branching program to output _n/_100 correct values, it must pass through at least one vertex _v_ such that (_v,L_) is good. If it didn’t, then either some node along the path outputs an incorrect value, or else we can divide the computation path into 2_T/n_ segments of length _n/_2, each of which outputs at most _n_<sup>2</sup>/400_T_ values, meaning at most _n/_200 outputs in total.

Now, note that, none of the computation paths from any of the start nodes can intersect each other, because otherwise one of them would fail to end up at the correct end node. Thus, in order for all _x_ of them to correctly solve unique elements on _L_, there must be at least _x_ good vertices.

These two claims together imply the overall result. By Claim 5.5, we have<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_{L\sim[n]^n}[\#\text{good vertices}]\le x2^S(1-\Omega(1))^{n^2/T}=x2^{S-\Omega(n^2/T)},\)

<tbc>meaning by Markov’s inequality that<tbc>

\(Pr_{L\sim[n]^n}[\#\text{good vertices}\ge x2^{S-\Omega(n^2/T)}]<1/2.\)

<tbc>But, observe that

\(Pr_{L\sim[n]^n}[L\text{has at least}n/100\text{unique elements}]>1/2.\)

So, there exists at least one value of _L_ such that the branching program has both fewer than \(x2^{S-\Omega(n^2/T)}\) good vertices and greater than _n/_100 unique elements. If we have \(ST\le o(n^2)\) (so \(S\le o(n^2/T)\)), then this would mean strictly fewer than _x_ good vertices, so Claim 5.6 would imply that the catalytic branching program is incorrect on _L_.

## A Quickly converting between registers over different moduli

For the remaining part of this appendix, we will fix an arbitrary modular ring K=Z_/m_Z representable in \(b:=\lceil logm\rceil\) bits. (We further assume \(O(logb)\le S\) for space _S_ algorithms.) We show that we can efficiently convert between catalytic algorithms which compute the output by adding it into _N_ registers over a modular ring Z_/m_Z and those which bitwise XOR the _N_-element output into dirty space (represented as _N_ concatenated _b_-bit blocks), and consequently registers over different moduli.

In the proofs below we will assume that all the _b_-bit dirty space chunks for any modular ring register represent a valid value in K (this is not always true when _m_ is not a power of two). We can use pre- processing and post-processing from the scheme of \[CDKMR26, Appendix A\] to assume this WLOG with only a poly(_b_)=polylog(_m_) time multiplicative overhead.

First, we use a simple helper lemma.

**Lemma A.1.** Assume there exists an algorithm which XORs a value \(v\in\{0,1\}^M\) onto a catalytic tape in time _T_, clean space _S_, and catalytic space _C_. Then, there exists an algorithm which adds \(v_i\in\{0,1\}\) to register _R<sub>i</sub>_ over K in the catalytic tape using time \(T\cdot\mathsf{polylog}(m)\), clean space _O(S_), and catalytic space _O(C_).

_Proof._ Allocate _M_ registers _R<sub>i</sub>_ over K in the catalytic tape. First, XOR the _i_th bit of the dirty space input section into the least significant bit (LSB) of _R<sub>i</sub>_ for all _i_. Run the catalytic algorithm XORing _v_ onto this chunk. XOR the _i_th bit into the LSB of _R<sub>i</sub>_ again. This procedure keeps _R<sub>i</sub>_ the same if _v<sub>i</sub>_=0 and adds \(\pm 1\) otherwise. In order to remove the negative sign, square the value added to each _R<sub>i</sub>_ by using \[BCKLS14\] transparent multiplication over K. Run these programs in parallel so only _O_(1) calls to the above \((0,\pm 1)\) procedure are used.

We can now show register modular ring output implies XOR output.

**Lemma A.2** (MOD _m_ to XOR)**.** Assume there exists an algorithm A adding vector \(v\in\mathcal{K}^N\) onto catalytic tape registers in time _T_, clean space _S_, and catalytic space _C_. Then, there exists an algorithm which bitwise XORs _v_ onto a block of catalytic tape in time \(T\cdot\mathsf{polylog}(m)\), clean space _O(S_), and catalytic space _O(C_).

_Proof._ Suppose the _Nb_-bit output dirty space block algorithm A uses is initialized to \(\tau\in\{0,1\}^{Nb}\). Let \(\tau_i\in\{0,1\}^b\) represent the initial _b_-bit value at register _R<sub>i</sub>_. Observe that by running A appropriately, we can<tbc>

toggle between having \(a:=(\tau_i)_{i\in[N]}\) or \(c:=(\tau_i+v_i)_{i\in[N]}\) in the catalytic tape.<sup>17</sup> In particular, we have read-access (and therefore XOR-access) to these values.

Allocate 2_Nb_ registers over Z/2_<sup>k</sup>_Z (for a _k_ discussed shortly). Add the _j_th bit of _a_ and _c_ onto _R_<sub>2_j_</sub> and _R_<sub>2_j_+1</sub> respectively for all _j_ using Lemma A.1, while only running A a constant number of times. (We can XOR the value of _a_ all at once onto any place in the catalytic tape. We can similarly do this for _c_ by toggling.) There exists an _NC_<sup>1</sup> circuit which given two values \(a_i,c_i\in\mathcal{K}\) finds _c<sub>i</sub>-a<sub>i</sub>_ over K. Let _k_ be the value needed for the power-of-two registers used in Theorem 1.1 for our circuit. Using Theorem 1.1, evaluate _N_ instances of this circuit in parallel in time \(O(T+N\cdot poly(b))\) and \(O(logb)\le O(S)\) additional space. As the output of the circuit evaluation will be in a bitwise XOR form, we can XOR the value \((c_i-a_i)_{i\in[N]}=(v_i)_{i\in[N]}\) onto a desired block.

**XOR-output to modular output.** We observe it is possible to go from XOR output to modular ring output with only a poly(_b_) overhead as well. This follows from first applying Lemma A.1 to add an XOR- access bit into a corresponding register in K (_Nb_ registers total); then, for each output ring register (_N_ total), accumulate the sum of the _k_th least significant bit register multiplied by 2_<sup>k</sup>_ over all _k_. (Do this in parallel over all output registers to maintain only a polylog(_m_) overhead.)

**Modulo _m_ output to modulo _a_ output.** We additionally observe that we can convert from an algorithm which adds values to registers mod _m_ to an algorithm which subsequently takes the remainder mod some other value.

**Lemma A.3** (MOD _m_ to MOD _a_)**.** Let _m,a_ be positive integers where 1_\<a\<m_, and \(v\in\mathbb{Z}^N\) be a vector where each entry has magnitude at most _a_ for all \(i\in[N]\). Assume there exists an algorithm adding vector _v_ onto catalytic tape registers over Z_/m_Z in time _T_, clean space _S_, and catalytic space _C_. There exists an algorithm running in time _T_polylog(_m_), clean space _O(S_), and catalytic space _O(C+N_polylog(_m_)) which instead adds _v_ over Z_/a_Z.

_Proof._ First, convert the added output over Z_/m_Z registers to XOR form by Lemma A.2. Then, convert to Z_/a_Z register form by the previous XOR to modular register output remark.

<sup>17</sup>To revert from \((\tau_i+v_i)_{i\in[N]}\) to \((\tau_i)_{i\in[N]}\) simply negate all the _N_ registers, run A, and negate all the registers again. This is a standard trick to get the inverse (i.e. subtract).
